clue.text: Ominous call in crossing the water

indicators.note: in tells us the word for call is placed inside the word for crossing the water

parts.note: wading across a river at a shallow place is fording it
a call at the card table or an auction is a bid

explanation.surface: A threatening cry is heard as someone wades across a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing the water' reads as a scene-setter but is the outer word, and 'in' is the container signal, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something menacing or threatening looks grim and unwelcoming, as an ominous sky does.

clue.text: An ass — as some would mention, a German ass

annotationWithheld.why: An ass — as some would mention, a German ass (6): no parse found that uses every word once; the homophone 'as some would mention' seems to need 'An' both as definition and as sounded fodder (ON + A + GER), a word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: An ass — as some would mention, a German ass

clue.text: A keen reader writing report about new work

indicators.note: about means the word for report goes round the other piece

parts.note: a report is a loud bang, a boom

indicators.note: new signals that the letters of work are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone who loves reading is writing a report on a recently published work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' is the anagram signal on 'work', and 'about' makes the bang go round it; 'writing' is only a link here, tempting as BOOK though it is not.
explanation.definitionFit: An avid, devoted reader is nicknamed after the grub said to eat through pages.

clue.text: Suffering, for having no locks

explanation.surface: Someone is upset because they have gone bald.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a whimsical reading: DIS- meaning removal, as in dismantle, plus TRESSED, having tresses or locks of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Suffering means troubled or anguished; having no locks plays on tresses, long locks of hair, being taken away.

clue.text: Popular feature of the church to fire the imagination

parts.note: popular means in, fashionable
a tall pointed tower on a church is its spire

explanation.surface: A well-liked church steeple stirs people's creativity.
explanation.definitionFit: To stimulate creative thought or enthusiasm in someone is to rouse their imagination.

clue.text: Note everything giving rise to irritation

parts.note: G is a note of the musical scale
everything means all

explanation.surface: A remark about everything starts to annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Gall is a sore made by chafing, hence vexation or annoyance.

clue.text: Legal claim certain to occasion amusement

parts.note: in court a plea is a formal claim or statement
certain means sure

explanation.surface: A court claim that is sure to win is cause for delight.
explanation.definitionFit: Enjoyment or delight taken in something is synonymous with amusement.

clue.text: He'll announce drivers' tea-break

indicators.note: break means the letters of drivers and tea are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A man announces that lorry drivers can stop for a cuppa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' looks like part of 'tea-break' but is the anagram signal on DRIVERS + TEA.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who publicises goods or notices in the press makes announcements to the public.

clue.text: A medico went ahead, but showed no inclination to hurry

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree
went ahead means led, as in going in front

explanation.surface: A doctor walks in front, but takes things slowly.
explanation.walkthrough: MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a crossword standard for a doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Walking at a slow, relaxed pace is the opposite of hurrying.

clue.text: Brave children — not the offspring of…

definitions.text: Brave children — not the offspring of…

parts.words: Brave children — not the offspring of…
parts.note: a brave is a Native American warrior, so his children are infants carried on the back, and the ellipsis runs into the next clue: not the children of white settlers

explanation.surface: Courageous youngsters, and not the sons of anyone ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brave' looks like an adjective (courageous), but it is a noun for a Native American warrior. The clue continues into 11-across.
explanation.definitionFit: A Native American baby or infant, carried strapped to its mother's back, is a brave's child.

clue.text: … run down old American?

parts.note: someone run down looks wan and colourless in the cheeks, and the old Western films have Native Americans calling white settlers by this name

explanation.surface: Completing the previous clue: a worn-out elderly person from the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: Read with 10-across: papooses are not the offspring of white people. 'run down' suggests looking pale, which is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: In old Westerns a white person, as seen by Native Americans, is named for their light skin.

clue.text: A lot of sailors love this river

parts.note: RN, the Royal Navy, is a whole body of sailors
love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Many seamen are fond of this particular waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: RN is the Royal Navy, Britain's navy. The river flows through Florence and Pisa in Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arno is a river in Tuscany, so it is named here by its category.

clue.text: Fool social workers without first making friends

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside means the first two pieces go around the word for first

parts.note: an ass is a fool
ants are social insects that live and work in colonies
first is written 1ST, and the 1 is read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A silly social worker is becoming friendly without making the first move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' and suggests a deleted letter, but in its old sense it means 'outside'.
explanation.definitionFit: Helpers or aides who give support are supporters, in the loose sense of friends.

clue.text: Real cuts or adjustments in a metropolitan area

indicators.note: adjustments means the letters of real cuts or are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Genuine reductions or tweaks are being made in a city district.
explanation.walkthrough: EARLS COURT is a district of west London, long known for its exhibition centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Earls Court is a district of west London, so it is an area of the capital city.

clue.text: To examine fanciful ideals can cause shock

parts.note: to scan is to examine closely

indicators.note: fanciful means the letters of ideals are treated imaginatively and rearranged

explanation.surface: Looking closely at idealistic notions can be very upsetting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fanciful' turns IDEALS into DALISE.
explanation.definitionFit: To outrage or offend people's sense of propriety is to shock them.

clue.text: "Let our frail thoughts dally with false ----" (Milton)

definitions.text: "Let our frail thoughts dally with false ----" (Milton)

parts.words: "Let our frail thoughts dally with false ----" (Milton)
parts.note: the line comes from Milton's elegy Lycidas, and the missing word means a guess or conjecture

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the line is from John Milton's poem Lycidas (1637), mourning a drowned friend.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing noun is a conjecture or supposition formed without firm evidence, fitting 'false' thoughts.

clue.text: A guide for the better sportsman

definitions.text: A guide for the better sportsman

parts.words: A guide for the better sportsman
parts.note: better reads as an improved player but means one who bets, and a race meeting's printed programme guides such a punter

explanation.surface: A handbook to help an athlete improve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' means a gambler here, not a superior player.
explanation.definitionFit: A printed list of the races and runners at a meeting guides those placing bets.

clue.text: To crowd round back of the goal would be folly

indicators.note: round means the word for crowd surrounds the other piece

parts.note: a crowd is a mass of people

indicators.note: back of here means the word for the goal is turned to run backwards

parts.note: the end is the goal or aim one works towards

explanation.surface: Bunching around the rear of the net would be a foolish move in football.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back of the goal' pretends to be a spot on a football pitch; 'back of' is the reversal signal and 'round' the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolish, senseless behaviour amounts to lunacy, as in 'it would be sheer lunacy'.

clue.text: Most disgusting drink is served in the snuggery

indicators.note: served in means the drink is placed inside the word for the snuggery

parts.note: a snuggery is a cosy retreat, a nest
Asti is a sparkling Italian wine

explanation.surface: A vile drink is being poured in the cosy back room of a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A snuggery (snug) is a small cosy room in a British pub; 'served in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of nasty means the most revolting or vile.

clue.text: In short cannot even find a place to eat

parts.note: cannot shortened is can't
even shortened in poetry is e'en

explanation.surface: In brief, one can't even find somewhere to have lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' tells you both words are contracted: CAN'T and the poetic E'EN.
explanation.definitionFit: A canteen is a dining hall in a factory, school or barracks.

clue.text: Support by an employee isn't new

parts.note: to support a motion is to second it
a hand is a worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: Backing from a member of staff is nothing original.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods previously owned by someone else are used, not fresh from the shop.

clue.text: Leading player stumped by a beginner in the end

parts.note: ST is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for stumped

indicators.note: in the end points to the final letter of the word beginner

explanation.surface: The team's top performer is dismissed by a novice at last.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman can be out 'stumped', written ST on the scorecard.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal performer in a film or play, or a team's best player, is its headliner.

clue.text: Lyrical recitative — A1, or so it might appear

indicators.note: it might appear suggests the letters shown look like the answer once moved into another order

parts.note: the figure 1 looks like the letter I

explanation.surface: A tuneful bit of opera seems first-rate, or so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 means first-class; read the 1 as I, then rearrange AI + OR + SO.
explanation.definitionFit: In opera a melodious passage between recitative and aria is a songlike recitative.

clue.text: Sort of current belief to accept as true

parts.note: AC, alternating current, is one kind of electric current
credit means belief or trust, as in giving credit to a story

explanation.surface: A kind of popular opinion that people take for granted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current' reads as 'present-day' with belief, but it is electrical current.
explanation.definitionFit: To believe or vouch for something, recognising it as genuine, is to give it credence.

clue.text: Underworld boss taking a large number round flat

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A gangland chief takes a big sum to the flat he lives in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld boss' suggests a mobster but means Dis, Roman ruler of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat circular object, like a plate or coin, is a thin round shape.

clue.text: Plant one, green or variegated

indicators.note: variegated, mixed in colour, suggests the letters of the pieces are mixed up

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Grow a single specimen, either plain green or with mottled leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variegated' is a gardener's word for multicoloured leaves, here the anagram signal for I + GREEN + OR.
explanation.definitionFit: Erigeron is a genus of daisy-like flowers, fleabane, so it is a kind of flowering herb.

clue.text: Drones seen from Barrie's window

explanation.surface: Male bees can be spotted from a writer's window.
explanation.walkthrough: J. M. Barrie, author of Peter Pan, wrote 'A Window in Thrums', named after his fictional version of his Scottish home town Kirriemuir.
explanation.definitionFit: Drones are monotonous humming sounds, as a strummed string makes; the second refers to Barrie's novel 'A Window in Thrums'.

clue.text: A meeting of traditionalists?

parts.note: the word for a formal assembly also names a custom or accepted practice, so it sounds like a gathering of those who follow custom

explanation.surface: A gathering of people who like things done the old way.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal assembly or conference shares its name with an established custom, which traditionalists observe.
